hints: Look closely at the four labels around the diagram: DNA, protein, 70S ribosomes and RNA. Which of these would you expect to find in a tiny particle made only of a nucleic acid core plus a coat?
Remember the golden rule for viruses: different viruses can have DNA or RNA as their genetic material, all have protein, but none have their own protein-making machinery.
walkthrough:
**Recall what a virus is built from**

Think of a virus as very simple and non-cellular. It is basically nucleic acid wrapped in a protein coat (the capsid, sometimes with an envelope).

It has no cytoplasm, no organelles and no ribosomes of its own.

**Check DNA, protein and RNA**

Feature 1 is DNA. Some viruses, e.g. adenovirus and bacteriophage lambda, have DNA as their genetic material. So 1 can be present.

Feature 2 is protein. All viruses have protein in their capsid. So 2 is present.

Feature 4 is RNA. Other viruses, e.g. influenza virus and HIV, have RNA as their genetic material. So 4 can be present.

**Rule out 70S ribosomes**

Feature 3 is 70S ribosomes. These are found in prokaryotic cells and in mitochondria and chloroplasts, not in viruses.

Viruses make no proteins themselves. They hijack the host cell ribosomes instead. So 3 is never present.

That leaves 1, 2 and 4.

options.A: Includes 70S ribosomes (3) which viruses never have, and misses RNA (4) which many viruses do have.
options.B: Correct. Viruses can have DNA (1) or RNA (4) depending on the type, and always have protein (2), but have no ribosomes.
options.C: Wrongly includes 70S ribosomes (3) and wrongly leaves out protein (2) which forms every viral capsid.
options.D: Wrongly includes 70S ribosomes (3) and wrongly leaves out DNA (1) which DNA viruses do contain.
